brief.head: Firms make the nation
brief.text: A rich coun­try is made of so­phis­ti­cated firms, Ajay Shah said. Policy can only set the con­di­tions; the real change lies in the cul­ture of India’s elite. {034-C11}

brief.head: Options for the boss
brief.text: A salaried CEO stays wary of risk, Ajay Shah said. Stock op­tions give a strong up­side: if the firm grows 5x or 10x, the CEO ben­e­fits big time. {#stockoptions}

brief.head: Execution as comfort
brief.text: Indian man­age­ments re­treat into ex­e­cu­tion, Ajay Shah said, be­cause strat­egy means fac­ing an un­pre­dictable world and mak­ing dif­fi­cult calls. Boards and ad­vi­sors should pull them out. {034-C09}

brief.head: Lost in a generation
brief.text: When a fam­ily be­comes wealthy, Amit Varma said, about 70 per cent of that wealth is lost by the next gen­er­a­tion, and 90 per cent by the one after. {034-C10}

brief.head: Exam-topper worship
brief.text: Ajay Shah mocked India’s rev­er­ence for exam top­pers: “the in­stinc­tive re­spect that some­body who could solve maths prob­lems in 12th stan­dard is a cool guy”. {034-J03}

thought.label: Thought for the day

thought.who: Ajay Shah, arguing that founders with everything in one firm become too timid

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s masterclass on the four designs of a firm
lead.head: Blame the design, not the family

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 34

body: In India, Ajay Shah said, busi­ness has a caste sys­tem. People look down on tra­di­tional busi­ness fam­i­lies and re­vere the pro­fes­sional who passed an IIT en­trance exam.

Shah called this the wrong way to think about the world. “We should think about in­cen­tives,” he said, “we should think about the forces that cre­ate good and bad de­ci­sions in­side firms.” {034-C01}
To prove it, he built a firm on air: Amitbhai Media Limited, owned and run, at first, by Amit Varma.
Each de­sign was judged on the same ques­tions. Are the own­ers and the man­agers aligned? Will the peo­ple in charge take risks? And how con­cen­trated is power?
## Four ways to run a firm
In Design One, Varma owns 100 per cent and is CEO. Alignment is per­fect, but with most of his wealth in one firm, he will be too timid to take big bets.
Nobody can tell him no, ei­ther. “In this firm, you are the lit­tle deity,” Shah said. {034-C02}

Design Two sells 40 per cent to out­siders, per­haps through an IPO. It is com­mon among listed Indian fam­ily firms, Shah said, and changes lit­tle: the founder stays cau­tious and un­chal­lenged, and can now take more than his share of the cash.
Design Three is the one the Indian elite ap­plauds. The fam­ily steps aside and hires a pro­fes­sional CEO on a salary, with no eq­uity. Shah was unim­pressed.

With no skin in the game, he said, the CEO spends the first three years try­ing not to be sacked and the rest coast­ing, while qui­etly gath­er­ing power. An IIT de­gree, Shah said, “doesn’t change things. It’s an in­cen­tives ques­tion.” {034-C05}
“We made it worse with de­sign two, and we made it even worse with de­sign three,” Varma said, and pleaded: “And now we need to get to de­sign four, please save Amitbhai Media Limited.”
## The board takes charge

Design Four, Shah said, is how large firms work all over the world. There is no pro­moter. Shares are spread among in­sti­tu­tions and the pub­lic, some­thing that has begun in India only in the last 10 or 15 years.

Shareholders choose a board of about seven: the CEO, roughly three di­rec­tors whose stakes mat­ter to them, and roughly three in­de­pen­dents. It sets strat­egy and or­gan­i­sa­tion de­sign, hires the CEO and holds the CEO to ac­count. {034-C06}
Sometimes the board makes life too hot for the CEO, who leaves. Shah called that healthy.
None of this can be writ­ten into law, he stressed. It is cul­ture, and it takes decades.
## The road from here
Varma asked how a real fam­ily firm should make the jour­ney, since it can­not reach Design Four overnight.

If some­one in the fam­ily has the hunger, Shah said, a fam­ily-led path beats hir­ing a pro­fes­sional. Power with an aligned fam­ily mem­ber is rel­a­tively safe; power with an unchecked hired man­ager is the worry. So build the board first, and only then bring in the out­sider. {034-C08}
That asks the in­cum­bent CEO to give up power, which is rare. Shah has sat on more than 20 boards and has seen, he said, “just dis­gust­ing lev­els of ar­ro­gance”.
Both hosts closed with fam­ily sagas: Shah with Thomas J Watson Jr’s IBM mem­oir, *Father, Son & Co*, and Varma with *The Godfather*, book and films.

second.label: Firms of one
second.head: Talking to the mirror
second.deck: Amit Varma finds his own career in Design One, flaws and all

pic.caption: Amit Varma on being a firm of one

body: Listening to Ajay Shah de­scribe a firm whose founder owns all of it and runs it, Amit Varma recog­nised him­self. Every cre­ator, he said, is an en­tre­pre­neur of his own brand, at once share­holder and CEO. {034-S03}

He likened him­self to Travis Bickle talk­ing to the mir­ror in *Taxi Driver*, then added: “I can’t act, of course.” {034-J07} The up­side is align­ment. He fol­lows his own vi­sion, and has passed up great op­por­tu­ni­ties to do the things he loves.

The cost is scale, and the lim­its of his own imag­i­na­tion and knowl­edge. Shah added that em­ploy­ees would not change that. “If you have em­ploy­ees, they don’t read­ily chal­lenge you enough be­cause you’re 100%.” {#challenge}

quote.text: I think of every cre­ator as being an en­tre­pre­neur of his own brand.

third.head: Even Jobs got it wrong

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the great-man myth

body: The busi­ness world loves a vi­sion­ary. It cred­its a firm’s suc­cess to a great CEO and blames fail­ure on a bad one. Ajay Shah thinks this at­tri­bu­tion is “pro­foundly wrong”.

Much of the out­come, he said, is dumb luck: being in the right in­dus­try at the right time, or the world sud­denly chang­ing. Steve Jobs, the busi­ness world’s favourite vi­sion­ary, made many wrong de­ci­sions. “He al­most took Apple into bank­ruptcy,” Shah said. {034-J08}

The world is in­fin­itely com­pli­cated, and no strong CEO un­der­stands it. “It is only by har­ness­ing many, many minds that we have a hope of un­der­stand­ing the world bet­ter,” he said. {034-C07}

When power is con­cen­trated in one per­son, he added, the qual­ity of de­ci­sions is gen­er­ally in­fe­rior. Indian busi­ness, he said later, is still stuck in a “prim­i­tive great man the­ory”. {#greatman}

p2.title: The firm, four ways
p2.deck: Ajay Shah builds Amitbhai Media Limited four times, and Amit Varma begs him to save it. {034-J02}

from1.head: Blame the design, not the family

quote.text: In this firm, you are the lit­tle deity, you are the God, you do all the think­ing, you make all the de­ci­sions.

box.title: What the research says
box.text: Amit Varma cited a Harvard Business Review ar­ti­cle, *What You Can Learn from Family Business*, and Ajay Shah agreed with ev­ery­thing in it. Professionally run firms do bet­ter in good times, it finds, but fam­ily firms do less badly in bad times. {034-R07}

sections.label: Design One
sections.head: One owner, no arguments
sections.caption: the founder who owns it all
body: Start with the sim­plest firm. Amit Varma owns 100 per cent of Amitbhai Media Limited and is also its CEO. There are many such firms all around us in India, Ajay Shah said.
What goes right is align­ment. The in­ter­ests of the firm, the CEO and the share­holder are one, and the owner will run hard.

What goes wrong is risk. With too much of the owner’s wealth in one firm, he be­comes cau­tious and in­vests only in small, in­cre­men­tal steps. Yet cap­i­tal­ism needs earth-shaking gam­bles, Shah said: some firms suc­ceed out­ra­geously, many die, “and that’s a good thing”. {034-C03}

Timid firms are not repo­si­tioned for the next wave of mar­kets and tech­nol­ogy, and are ren­dered ir­rel­e­vant as the years go by. The flaw, Shah said, is not that the per­son is a bad one. It is the stance on risk.
## Nobody to say no

The sec­ond dif­fi­culty is con­cen­trated power. With no check and bal­ance, and no­body to force ar­gu­ments be­fore de­ci­sions, bad de­ci­sions are made, money is wasted and wrong projects are taken up. {034-C02}
Hiring staff would not fix it, he added. Employees rarely chal­lenge some­one who owns 100 per cent.
~ Many peo­ple start with this de­sign, Shah said, and hope­fully evolve out of it into a bet­ter firm.

quote.text: In this firm, you are the lit­tle deity, you are the God, you do all the think­ing, you make all the de­ci­sions.

sections.label: Design Two
sections.head: Same boss, new partners
sections.caption: selling 40 per cent to outsiders
body: In Design Two, Amit Varma keeps 60 per cent and stays CEO, while two mi­nor­ity share­hold­ers, Vaishnav and Nomsita, take 20 per cent each. It may even be a listed com­pany. Ajay Shah said this is a very com­mon de­sign among Indian fam­ily firms.

Alignment stays high. The founder is slightly more di­ver­si­fied, but 60 per cent of the firm is still likely to be the big­gest thing on his bal­ance sheet, and his ego and stand­ing are bound up in it. So he stays risk-averse. {#ego}
Power is as con­cen­trated as be­fore. The 40 per cent have none.
## A new prob­lem
Particularly in India, Shah said, a 60 per cent owner can ex­tract more than 60 per cent of the cash. {#extract} Investors who ex­pect less than their share will pay less for the shares.

Most of India’s com­pany law and SEBI rules for listed firms fight this one bat­tle, he said. It is a fair ques­tion, but the de­bate has missed the big­ger flaws: an under-diversified owner with ex­ces­sive power. {034-C04}
~ “You are un­shak­able,” Shah told Varma. “There is no de­bate, there is no dis­cus­sion.”

quote.text: This is the one ques­tion that has oc­cu­pied the Indian imag­i­na­tion.

sections.label: Design Three
sections.head: The CEO with no skin
sections.caption: the salaried professional CEO
body: Design Three, Ajay Shah said, is the one loved by the Indian elite. Amit Varma keeps 60 per cent but steps aside, and a so-called pro­fes­sional from IIT is hired as CEO, on a salary and with no eq­uity.
Varma re­minded “gen­tle read­ers” that Shah is him­self from IIT. “This is most in­sid­i­ous,” he said, “but con­tinue.” {034-J04}
The new CEO has no skin in the game. Hired for a five-year term, the pro­fes­sional thinks: “The one thing I don’t want is to be sacked at the end of three years.” {#sacked}
So the first three years go on cost con­trol and in­cre­men­tal im­prove­ments. Then the CEO squeaks through to a sec­ond term, and coasts to ten years with­out rock­ing the boat.
## Same prob­lems, plus one

The chair­man, who hires the CEO and can fire them, keeps nudg­ing them away from risk, and is un­likely to be stopped from tak­ing extra cash. And the CEO con­sol­i­dates power in­side the firm, with no­body to ques­tion them. {#powercorrupts}
~ If the fam­ily steps back in, the gos­sip col­umns say the pro­fes­sional is not in charge. “Either way, it’s a mug’s game,” Shah said.

quote.text: You’ve given power to a per­son with­out skin and it works pretty badly.

sections.label: Design Four
sections.head: Seven people in a room
sections.caption: the board that runs the firm
body: Design Four is how large, com­plex firms work all over the world, Ajay Shah said. There is no pro­moter. Shares are spread among in­sti­tu­tions and the pub­lic, and that has begun in India only in the last 10 or 15 years. {#dispersed}
The share­hold­ers pick a board. On a good one sit the CEO, about three share­holder di­rec­tors whose 5 to 15 per cent stakes mat­ter to them, and about three in­de­pen­dent di­rec­tors.
The board de­bates and ap­proves the firm’s strat­egy and its or­gan­i­sa­tion de­sign. {034-C06} It hires the CEO and con­trols the CEO’s pay.
## Heat in the board­room
“Why are we not win­ning? Why is our com­peti­tor doing bet­ter?” the board asks. Sometimes it is too hot for the CEO, who leaves, and Shah called that good and healthy. {#toohot}

Stock op­tions give the CEO a strong up­side, and di­ver­si­fied share­hold­ers can ac­cept that some firms will fail. When what sounded like a cat screamed in the back­ground, Amit Varma ex­plained it as “a CEO who had been ejected by the an­i­mal be­hav­iour of an un­ruly board”. {034-J05}
~ None of this can be cod­i­fied in laws, Shah stressed. It is cul­ture, and it takes decades for a coun­try to evolve to this kind of power re­la­tion­ship.

quote.text: But the strat­egy of the firm is con­trolled by the board, where the CEO is a mem­ber.

sections.label: Getting there
sections.head: Build the board first
sections.caption: the road from family firm to Design Four
body: The leap from Design Three to Design Four, Amit Varma said, is far vaster than the steps be­fore it. And mak­ing a for­tune is no guar­an­tee of keep­ing it: about 70 per cent of a family’s new wealth is lost by the next gen­er­a­tion. {034-C10}
He thought of the Nehrus, who “got lesser and lesser as peo­ple”, and of the Ambanis. “Every Dhirubhai is not going to have a Mukesh,” he said. {034-J11}

Ajay Shah agreed that the pro­fes­sional is no panacea, and that fam­ily mem­bers are not bad peo­ple. Where the fam­ily has a suc­ces­sor with the hunger, he would favour a fam­ily-led path to­wards Design Four.
## The order of things
First spread the share­hold­ing, he ad­vised, and build the board as an in­sti­tu­tion, with three share­holder di­rec­tors and three in­de­pen­dents. Only then bring in the hired CEO. {034-C08}
Strategy ad­vi­sors help too, by chal­leng­ing man­age­ments that would rather stick to ex­e­cu­tion. “You go home and watch TV, you don’t have to think too much,” Shah said. {034-C09}

~ Some fam­i­lies have no choice. When ven­ture cap­i­tal and pri­vate eq­uity in­vestors exit after an IPO, Shah said, the firm ends up with dis­persed share­hold­ers and must make Design Four work. {#vc}

quote.text: When a fam­ily be­comes wealthy, 70% of that wealth is lost by the next gen­er­a­tion, 90% is lost by the gen­er­a­tion after that.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the road from family firm to Design Four

quote.text: The story of India’s emer­gence from being a poor coun­try to our dreams of be­com­ing a rich coun­try is en­tirely in the firms. A rich coun­try is made of so­phis­ti­cated firms. A poor coun­try is made of bad firms.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A thank-you note, a help desk, an IBM gamble and a film class

stories.kicker: A student’s message, two decades in the making
stories.head: The thank-you that took 20 years
body: Three months be­fore the episode, Amit Varma was in Delhi, and one of his writ­ing stu­dents, Uja Sharma, recorded a mes­sage for Ajay Shah on Varma’s phone. She in­sisted it be played on the show, so Varma played it live, to catch Shah’s re­ac­tion.

Around 2000 or 2001, Sharma was a final-year stu­dent at the College of Business Studies in Delhi University, doing a project on fu­tures and op­tions. Ninety per cent of her re­search ma­te­rial, she said, bore Shah’s name. {#ninety}
She emailed him, not ex­pect­ing to hear back. He replied promptly, and on a video call, on what­ever plat­form the day of­fered, they talked for more than an hour.
Shah ex­plained how de­riv­a­tives worked, how the pol­icy was com­ing to­gether and what the NSE was doing. She went back, she said, “a lot smarter”, and aced the sub­ject.
The les­son out­lasted the exam. Making time for young peo­ple, she said, had stayed with her. “Every time a young per­son reaches out to me, I make time for them now.” {034-S01}
Shah, watch­ing, had no mem­ory of any of it. He had, he said, done this a lot.

~ Varma was not sur­prised. It clearly hap­pened, he said, and it was ex­actly the kind of thing Shah does, going out of his way to help peo­ple when he has no rea­son to. “I im­me­di­ately said, yeah, yeah, that’s very much the guy.”
stories.why: A video call of an hour, two decades ago, made Sharma some­one who makes time for the young. Small acts of in­tel­lec­tual gen­eros­ity can shape a per­son for decades with­out the giver ever know­ing, and get passed on.
stories.postscript: Shah an­swered with a story of his own, about how strangers’ emails turned him into a help desk.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Uja Sharma’s thank-you

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the emails that found him his calling
stories.head: A help desk by divine decree
body: In the late 1990s, Ajay Shah said, de­riv­a­tives trad­ing was on the rise in Indian fi­nance. He taught sem­i­nars all over the coun­try, and did tu­to­rial-style con­ver­sa­tions on tele­vi­sion that were played over and over, twice a day. {#tv} Many peo­ple came to see him as the teacher of de­riv­a­tives.
Then the emails started. Strangers de­scribed their plans and their prob­lems, and asked him to fix them. At first he was taken aback: he was not going to debug other people’s work.
“But by the fifth email, I got the mes­sage that the good Lord had in­tended for me to be a help desk,” he said. {034-S02}
~ So he de­cided to dis­charge his dharma, and has faith­fully replied to all of them ever since. He still tries to make time for PhD stu­dents and early-stage aca­demics.
stories.why: When the same kind of re­quest keeps ar­riv­ing at your door, it may be telling you where you are most use­ful. Accepting that role, as Shah did, can qui­etly do a lot of pub­lic good.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on becoming a help desk

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s pick: a family-business memoir from IBM
stories.head: The son who bet the house
body: Thomas J Watson Jr in­her­ited IBM from his fa­ther, its founder. When the son started out, Ajay Shah said, IBM was “a funny feu­dal com­pany where every morn­ing peo­ple woke up and sang the com­pany an­them”.

The son bet on the world’s most ex­pen­sive op­er­at­ing sys­tem project, OS/360. {034-S04} In in­fla­tion-adjusted dol­lars, Shah said, it cost more than the Manhattan Project, and Watson led IBM through it all.
Watson told the story in *Father, Son & Co*, which Shah read when he was young. It is a pure fam­ily-business book, he said, about Designs One and Two, and a beau­ti­fully writ­ten one.
~ Earlier in the episode, Shah had said that the only way to build a great busi­ness is to roll the dice, and that founders with ev­ery­thing rid­ing on one firm rarely dare. {034-C03}

quote.text: And Tom Watson Jr, the son, rolled the dice on the world’s most ex­pen­sive op­er­at­ing sys­tem project.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Tom Watson Jr’s gamble

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s pick, and a memory from Channel V
stories.head: Coppola in the promos room
body: Between 1995 and 1997, Amit Varma worked at Channel V, his sec­ond job. {#channelv} A film­maker there, Shamin Desai, who sadly died a few years ago, gath­ered a few peo­ple from the pro­mos de­part­ment for a lit­tle film ap­pre­ci­a­tion ses­sion.
With a dinky lit­tle recorder, Desai gave a talk. Francis Ford Coppola, he ex­plained, made *Rumblefish* at the same time as *The Outsiders*, with pretty much the same cast.
“And he said *Rumblefish* is a mas­ter­piece, spoke all about it, and played it,” Varma re­called. There were just five or six of them in the room. {034-S05}

~ Varma called it a mas­ter­class in film ap­pre­ci­a­tion, and added *Rumblefish* to his picks, after *The Godfather*, book and films. Everything Ajay Shah says about good cor­po­rate cul­ture, he said, “was right there in that room”.
stories.why: A se­nior col­league tak­ing the time to teach ju­niors, Varma sug­gested, is what good cor­po­rate cul­ture looks like. It is the same les­son as Shah’s help desk and Uja Sharma’s mes­sage: make time for the young.

quiz.q: What did Uja Sharma learn from Ajay Shah’s hour-long video call, beyond how derivatives work?
quiz.a: To make time for young peo­ple when­ever they reach out to her.

quiz.q: In Design One, why does a founder who owns 100 per cent take too few risks?
quiz.a: Too much of their wealth is locked in one firm: they are under-diversified.

quiz.q: Which single problem, according to Shah, do most Indian company law and SEBI rules try to fix?
quiz.a: Making sure mi­nor­ity share­hold­ers get their fair share of the firm’s cash.

quiz.q: Why does a salaried professional CEO spend the first three years of a five-year term playing safe?
quiz.a: Being sacked after three years would de­stroy their ca­reer, so they avoid risk.

quiz.q: On a Design Four board of about seven, who sits alongside the CEO?
quiz.a: Roughly three share­holder di­rec­tors with mean­ing­ful stakes and three in­de­pen­dent di­rec­tors.

quiz.q: What did Tom Watson Jr bet IBM on, and how big was the bet?
quiz.a: OS/360, which in in­fla­tion-adjusted dol­lars cost more than the Manhattan Project.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 34. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Thomas Watson (U.S. State department, public domain); Mario Puzo (Bernard Gotfryd, public domain); Francis Ford Coppola (The White House, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

laughs.text: Ajay’s run­ning ex­am­ple is the fic­tional ‘Amitbhai Media Limited’. After Designs Two and Three each make things worse, Amit pleads: ‘And now we need to get to de­sign four, please save Amitbhai Media Limited.’
After a cat-like scream is heard in the back­ground, Amit tells lis­ten­ers it wasn’t a cat: ‘It was a wail­ing of a CEO who had been ejected by the an­i­mal be­hav­ior of an un­ruly board.’

When Ajay in­stantly pro­duces a copy of The Godfather, Amit is stunned: ‘Oh you have it. What the fuck? You have ev­ery­thing here.’ He won­ders whether Ajay owns some­thing that looks like a book but has a screen, so any book Amit names just ap­pears on it.
Steve Jobs as the poster child of the vi­sion­ary-CEO myth. Ajay’s re­but­tal: ‘Steve Jobs made many, many wrong de­ci­sions. He al­most took Apple into bank­ruptcy.’
Dhirubhai and Mukesh Ambani: ‘every Dhirubhai is not going to have a Mukesh. You know, that was just get­ting ex­traor­di­nar­ily lucky.’
